title: From Delhi to a $1.7 Billion Valuation: How Ritu Narayan Built Zūm to Fix America's Broken School Bus System
excerpt: The Indian-origin founder left eBay to tackle the country's largest — and most outdated — mass transit system. A decade later, Zūm serves 4,500 schools and just hit unicorn status.
body:
• Ritu Narayan, who grew up in Delhi and studied computer engineering as one of six women in a class of 300, founded Zūm after struggling with school transportation as a working mom at eBay.
  • Zūm recently raised $100 million from TPG's Rise Fund, valuing the company at $1.7 billion with total funding of $430 million.
  • The platform now serves over 4,500 schools across 17 states, generated $333 million in revenue in 2025, and has surpassed $2 billion in total contract value.
  • Narayan has been named an EY Entrepreneur of the Year 2026 Bay Area finalist and recognized by Fast Company, CNBC Disruptor 50, and the World Economic Forum.

Ritu Narayan was a group product manager at eBay when the daily puzzle of getting her two young children to and from school nearly pushed her out of her career. It was a problem she recognized from a generation earlier — her mother, an educator in Delhi, had quit her own job to raise Narayan and her three siblings full-time.

"As a working parent, I struggled to get my kids safely and efficiently to and from school," Narayan told Pulse 2.0. "I had seen my mother face the same issue three decades ago when I was a child in India."

That generational frustration became the seed for Zūm, the student transportation company Narayan founded in 2015 that just crossed the $1.7 billion valuation mark after a $100 million investment from TPG's Rise Fund.

From Delhi to Silicon Valley

Narayan grew up in Delhi as the oldest of four children. She was the first female computer engineer in her extended family, earning her degree from the Delhi Institute of Technology — one of just six women in a 300-person program. She moved to the United States in 1999, working as a management consultant at IBM and PricewaterhouseCoopers before moving into product management roles at Oracle, Yahoo, and eventually eBay.

https://x.com/Forbes/status/2089261159514034496

Along the way, she earned a master's degree from Stanford Graduate School of Business. But it was the collision of her career ambitions with the reality of American school logistics that changed her trajectory.

"It was an 'aha' moment for me that this problem is universal, this problem is generational, and nothing has been built to solve it," Narayan said in an LTSE podcast interview.

Reinventing America's Largest Mass Transit System

Student transportation in the United States moves 26 million children to school every day, making it the country's largest mass transit system. Yet most of it still runs on walkie-talkies, clipboards, and routing systems that haven't changed in decades. The dysfunction adds up: more than half of parents say their children feel anxious about school transportation, and the ripple effects cost an estimated $15 billion in lost learning each year, according to Zūm's research.

Narayan initially launched Zūm as an "Uber for kids" — a direct-to-parent rideshare with certified drivers. But she quickly realized the real opportunity was far larger. In 2019, the company pivoted to partner directly with school districts, replacing their entire transportation operations with an integrated technology platform covering route optimization, fleet management, driver coordination, and real-time tracking.

"Student transportation is not just about transportation. It's about access to education."

— Ritu Narayan, Founder and CEO of Zūm

The results have been measurable. Zūm reports a 98% on-time performance rate, a 4.9-star parent satisfaction rating across 1.7 million reviews, and an 86% reduction in transportation-related absences in districts like Kansas City Public Schools. In San Francisco, districts using the system have cut annual transportation costs by up to 10%.

A $1.7 Billion Valuation and Breakeven

The $100 million investment from TPG's Rise Fund — its impact-focused arm — brings Zūm's total funding to $430 million from investors including Sequoia, GIC, and SoftBank. The deal values the company at $1.7 billion, up from $1.3 billion at its 2024 Series E round. TPG Managing Partner Steve Ellis has joined Zūm's board.

Zūm generated $333 million in revenue in 2025, a 35% year-over-year increase, with a four-year revenue CAGR exceeding 40%. The company has surpassed $2 billion in total contract value and reached breakeven on an adjusted EBITDA basis — a milestone in a $50 billion market that remains highly fragmented.

"This business is operating in a very large, $50-billion, highly fragmented market," Ellis said. "None of the existing legacy operators have built a modern, fully integrated technology stack. It creates a real right to win."

Electric Buses and Energy Innovation

Zūm has also pushed into electric school buses, launching the nation's first all-electric, vehicle-to-grid (V2G) school bus fleet in Oakland. The company is expanding that effort in San Francisco with what it calls the largest electric school bus deployment in the country. Its buses double as distributed energy assets, feeding power back to the electric grid during off-hours.

Today, Zūm serves more than 4,500 schools across 17 states, including major districts like Los Angeles Unified, Boston Public Schools, San Francisco Unified, Omaha Public Schools, and Kansas City Public Schools. An IPO remains a possibility down the line, though Narayan has said organic growth is the priority.

Narayan's leadership has earned recognition from Fast Company's Most Innovative Companies list, CNBC's Disruptor 50, and the World Economic Forum. She was recently named an EY Entrepreneur of the Year 2026 Bay Area finalist.

"Being named a finalist for Entrepreneur Of The Year is a reflection of what happens when you refuse to accept that a broken system is inevitable."

— Ritu Narayan

For the Indian-origin founder who once watched her mother give up a career because of the same problem she later set out to solve, the $1.7 billion milestone marks validation of a decade-long bet. But Narayan's ambition stretches further: "Our ultimate goal is to bring Zūm to all 26 million students who are taking student transportation every single day," she told Reuters.
